article_text:
Archives – November 2, 2022

German photographer Ilse Bing (1899-1998) has secured her place as one of the major photographers of the 20th century. Her pioneering images during the inter-war era reveal a modern vision influenced by the impact of both the Bauhaus and Surrealism. Alongside her personal work she produced images in the fields of photojournalism, architectural photography, advertising and fashion, and her work was published in the major magazines of the period and exhibited in France and Germany. She moved from Frankfurt to Paris in 1931 but when the city was taken by the Germans during World War II she and her husband, who were both Jews, were expelled and interned in the South of France. They emigrated to New York in 1941 and she lived there until her death in 1998.

Since the 1970s when she first exhibited at MOMA, New York, there has been a burgeoning interest in her work and, more generally, in European photography of the 1920s and 1930s. As one of the key creative forces of the period Bing became a frequent speaker on the photography of that time and on the development of modern art.

This book, published in association with Fundacion MAPFRE, coincides with a comprehensive retrospective of her work being shown in Madrid by MAPFRE from September 2022 to January 2023. The book offers a chronological and thematic survey of her intense creative career and includes over 160 photographs as well as texts by leading experts Juan Vicente Aliaga, Benjamin Buchloh and Donna West Brett.

article_text:
奈良美智、2027年秋にSFMOMAで大規模展を開催。約100点を通して創作世界の変遷をたどる

2027年秋に 奈良美智 の大規模回顧展が サンフランシスコ近代美術館 で開催される。北カリフォルニア初となる包括的な回顧展には、絵画や彫刻、写真など、代表作約100点が集結する。

サンフランシスコ近代美術館 （San Francisco Museum of Modern Art、以下SFMOMA）は、2027年秋に 奈良美智 の大規模回顧展を開催すると 発表した 。奈良の創作活動を包括的に紹介する回顧展としては、北カリフォルニアで初めてとなる。

キュレーションは、SFMOMA絵画・彫刻部門のアソシエイト・キュレーター、ナンシー・リムと、ロサンゼルスを拠点とする吉竹美香がゲストキュレーターとして担当する。戦後・現代日本美術を専門とする吉竹は、 ロサンゼルス・カウンティ美術館 （LACMA）の奈良美智回顧展（2021-2022）や、香港の M＋ で行われた 草間彌生 の大規模回顧展「Yayoi Kusama: 1945 to Now」（2022-2023）などを手がけてきた。

本展では、同館7階の展示室を会場に、絵画、ドローイング、彫刻、インスタレーション、サウンド、写真など約100点が集結する。目玉となるのは、今回が初の海外展示となる《Voyage of the Moon（Resting Moon）》（2006）だ。奈良のドローイング制作アトリエを思わせる小屋の屋根には、大きな月の顔がひと休みするかのように置かれている。幼い頃から夜空に魅了されてきた奈良の想像力が反映された作品で、2020〜2021年には東京・ 森美術館 で開催された「STARS展：現代美術のスターたち―日本から世界へ」でも展示された。

本展では、こうした幼少期の記憶に根ざした作品に加え、東日本大震災以降に見られる奈良の表現の変化にも光を当てる。

SFMOMAによると、2011年の震災と福島第一原発事故を経て、奈良の作品は内省的な性格をいっそう強めたという。幾重にも重なる絵の具の層や、にじむような筆致、何かを探し求めるような人物のまなざしが特徴的な絵画に加え、手作業の痕跡や不完全さが残る近年の彫刻などを通じて、奈良の創作世界の変遷をたどる。

article_text:
Arpita Singh , an Indian painter whose hallucinatory work fused allusions to real-world violence with uninterpretable dream imagery, died on Monday in New Delhi. She was 89, according to a report by the Tribune that cited confirmation from her husband, the artist Paramjit Singh.

Singh frequently switched her technique and way of working across her six-decade-long career, though she is today most well-known for hallucinatory figurative paintings that are steeped in Hindu lore and Indian history. In her most famous paintings, gods and laypeople appear to float through the air in landscapes that vaguely recall maps.

Devi Pistol Wali (1990), arguably her most widely discussed painting, features a shrouded woman with many arms, one of which holds a gun to a man holding a sword. The painting has typically been described as a response to violence against women in modern-day India, but Singh discouraged these interpretations, saying that current events “come into my painting like the way light comes as colour and breeze comes as movement,” as she put it in a 2025 Guardian interview .

She also tended to rebut the repeated description of her work as dreamlike, since she could control what went into her art. “Her paintings are not dreamworlds—they are real worlds of her own creation,” wrote Meara Sharma in an Artforum essay on Devi Pistol Wali . “In the worlds of her paintings, objects do not ‘float,’ because gravity does not exist.”

Singh was one of the most high-profile Indian contemporary artists, with the artist receiving the esteemed Padma Bhushan award in 1991. The Kiran Nadar Museum of Art in New Delhi organized a retrospective of her work in 2019.

But outside India, Singh was not widely known until 2025, when the Serpentine Galleries staged a survey of her work in London. “An admired artist in India, Arpita Singh rarely shows in America and that is our loss,” wrote critic John Yau in a 2017 Hyperallergic review of an exhibition at New York’s Talwar Gallery, one of the few exhibitions of her work staged outside India that is listed on her CV. (Talwar is currently staging another Singh show, on view through February 27.)

Singh did not seem entirely fazed by the recent international reception of her work, however. In her Guardian profile, she merely called the Serpentine exhibition “a prestigious thing for me.”

Arpita Singh was born in 1937 in West Bengal, India, and moved in 1946 to New Delhi. Partition, the violent cleaving of British India into a Hindu-majority India and a Muslim-majority Pakistan, happened the following year and shaped some of Singh’s early memories. She recalled standing on her balcony and observing as a man was killed below.

She went on to attend Delhi Polytechnic’s art school, from which she graduated in 1959. Her teachers included modernists such as Biren De and Sailoz Mookherjea, and her education brought her into contact with books on European modernism. She recalled gravitating toward Der Blaue Reiter, Wassily Kandinsky, Paul Klee, and Marc Chagall.

Though Singh found success relatively early on in her career, showing with the dealer Kekoo Gendhy, who had helped make S. H. Raza and M. F. Husain famous, she felt uncertain about her figurations, which were done in a faux naive style. During the 1970s and ’80s, she started working in abstraction, producing austere, largely colorless images formed entirely from dots and dashes. By the end of the ’80s, however, she had returned to figuration.

There are signs that Singh is gradually growing in prominence. In 2021, her work appeared in a blockbuster exhibition of abstractions by women at the Centre Pompidou in Paris and that year’s edition of the Gwangju Biennale in South Korea. The next year, she showed at the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, India’s top contemporary art exhibition.

What became obvious as Singh grew more internationally famous was that few others have produced work like hers, both when she started and now. “I control the law,” Singh once said, speaking of the worlds she creates in her art. “I’m the master.”

article_text:
Internazionale and Milan have unveiled plans for their new Generali Stadium, which will replace the shared San Siro venue from the 2031-32 season.

The stadium, sponsored by Generali – Italy’s largest insurance company – will have a capacity of 71,500 seats and is expected to cost the two clubs €1.2 billion (£1bn). The plans were revealed at a gala event at Milan’s Castello Sforzesco on Thursday – but some fans in attendance voiced their opposition to San Siro being demolished.

Shortly before the briefing began, a group of Inter fans walked into the courtyard of the castle and unfurled a banner reading “you will never extinguish the lights at San Siro,” and chanting “hands off San Siro.” Work on the new stadium is set to begin in 2028, on the site of the existing 75,000-capacity venue.

The Generali Stadium will be shaped “low in the body, and rises up at either end” behind the goals, architect Norman Foster said. David Manica, a stadium specialist who collaborated with Foster on the project, added that the steep-sided design aims to bring fans as close to the pitch as possible.

“The most important thing that we realised when we designed this project is that San Siro is a feeling,” Manica said. “It’s more than a building, it’s a feeling … we brought all the seats as close as possible to the field. They could not be any closer, it’ll actually feel as though you’re sitting on the grass.”

The stadium will also be capable of hosting NFL international games, rugby matches and concerts. Milan and Inter paid €197 million (£165m) to acquire the current San Siro stadium and its adjacent parking arenas. The current ground will be largely demolished once construction work nears completion.

Also known as the Giuseppe Meazza Stadium, San Siro opened in 1926 and is the largest sports stadium in Italy. It is considered to be one of European football’s most iconic venues, but requires extensive modernisation despite undergoing a number of renovations during its lifespan.

after newsletter promotion

The Generali Stadium could be used as a venue for Euro 2032, which is being jointly hosted by Italy and Turkey. Foster and Manica previously worked together on the new Wembley Stadium, while the architect’s Foster + Partners firm also designed the plans for Manchester United’s proposed new 100,000-capacity home.

article_text:
The American French Film Festival , which celebrated its 30th anniversary this year, has been on a journey to cultivate a new generation of French movie lovers for two decades with its educational program for Los Angeles high school students.

This milestone edition brought around 3,000 students to the DGA theater for five packed screenings of “In Waves,” Phuong Mai Nguyen’s heart-wrenching animated feature which was bought Netflix at Cannes.

Adapted from AJ Dungo’s graphic novel at set in Southern California, “In Waves” is a love story between a shy teenage boy and the girl who teaches him how to surf and how to live, before she succumbs to cancer.

The screenings, which drew applause and tears throughout, also gave students the opportunity to engage in the post-screening Q&A with the film’s producer, Priscilla Bertin , and screenwriter Fanny Burdino.

Spearheaded by Anouchka Van Riel , the festival deputy director, the program brings together more than 60 schools over five days, with roughly half coming from the public school system and half from private institutions. It also reaches beyond French-language classes to students studying performing arts and other creative disciplines.

In an interview with Variety , Van Riel discussed the importance of the programme to allow younger audiences to discover international cinema at a time when arthouse moviegoers are aging and foreign-language films face growing challenges in U.S. theaters. She also talked about the program’s rapid growth, why subtitles are no longer the barrier they once were, and the powerful response to “In Waves” which Netflix is positioning in the Awards race.

How many students and schools participate in the program?

We have more than 60 schools participating over five days, so that’s more than 12 schools a day. We organize five screenings of the same film, each with around 600 students. That’s approximately 3,000 students every year. I’ve built a database of around 300 schools, and we start reaching out in May. Within a week of sending the first email, half the seats — around 1,500 — are already booked. Then I spend the summer filling the remaining places. There’s enormous demand. We also make a point of having a mix of public and private schools, roughly 50/50. That’s very important to us. For public schools, transportation can be a challenge. Some have to apply for grants just to pay for the buses. There’s an entire economy around organizing these trips, and a lot depends on the teachers.

How does the festival work with teachers to prepare students for the screenings?

We work with the American Association of Teachers of French, which prepares two educational guides, one in French and one in English. The French-language guide is around 100 pages long. It’s incredibly detailed and allows teachers to explore the film from multiple perspectives, including its themes and cinematic language. The guides are designed to help students study the film before or after the screening. And we don’t just work with French-language classes. Around half of the participating classes are English-speaking. Many Los Angeles high schools have performing arts programs, and those students come because they’re interested in cinema and want to meet the filmmakers. The majority of these kids have never attended a film screening followed by a Q&A. That’s something we want to change.

That’s surprising in Los Angeles, where the film industry is everywhere.

It’s extraordinary. I’m a member of the Producers Guild, and I receive invitations to screenings and conversations with filmmakers almost every day. There are incredible events happening constantly, but these kids don’t have access to them. Of course, if their parents work in the industry, that’s different. But otherwise, most students aren’t exposed to that world. I grew up in a small town in Alsace, and I remember my French teacher taking us to the movies all the time when I was in middle school. Some of those screenings even had Q&As. There’s a tradition of that in France that doesn’t really exist here in the same way. We used to organize masterclasses for university students, including at USC, but we realized it was difficult to attract them. They’re already surrounded by so many opportunities on campus. With high school students, we can work directly through the teachers. That’s how we’ve developed this program.

Is the goal ultimately to cultivate a younger audience for French cinema?

Absolutely. It’s about renewing the audience. A couple of years ago, we screened “The Marching Band,” and when the film was eventually released theatrically in the U.S., I was invited to moderate a Q&A. I loved the film, so I was very happy to do it. But the theater was only half full, and I don’t think there was a single person under 65. That’s the problem. Foreign-language films have traditionally been considered niche in the U.S. Streaming platforms have helped change that perception somewhat, but we still need to familiarize younger audiences with these films. That’s why this program is so important.

Are subtitles still an obstacle for younger American audiences?

Not nearly as much as people think. We’ve conducted surveys with students after the screenings, and more than 80% say subtitles aren’t a barrier to watching foreign-language films. It’s not a completely scientific study, but it gives us a good indication of how attitudes are changing. Between streaming platforms, social media and series like “Squid Game,” young people have become accustomed to watching subtitled content. Sometimes there’s still a little hesitation before the screening. But once they’re sitting in the theater, they realize it’s easy. I really don’t think subtitles are the problem for this generation anymore. Distribution is a major part of the problem. That’s why streaming platforms have become so important for the circulation of foreign-language films. But there’s also the question of exposure. If young people aren’t given opportunities to discover these films, they’re not necessarily going to seek them out themselves.

This year’s selection was “In Waves.” What made it particularly suitable for the program?

There’s a wonderful connection between this film and the festival. The producer, Priscilla Bertin, had already come to the festival two years ago with “Wild Diamond,” and at the time she was in post-production on “In Waves.” We became familiar with the project very early, and it made complete sense for us to bring it back this year. What’s interesting is that the film is based on an American graphic novel that was discovered by a French producer in a secondhand bookstore in France and developed into a movie. We explain that background to the students before the screenings, including why it’s considered a French film and the response has been extraordinary.

The screenings were packed, and the students seemed particularly moved by the film. What was the atmosphere like?

It was very striking. At the first screening, I went straight into introducing the filmmakers for the Q&A, and I realized something wasn’t right because the students were still processing what they’d just watched. Usually, when a film ends, the students immediately line up to ask questions. But with “In Waves,” it took time. Every day, there was this moment of silence. The film had affected them so deeply that they needed a little time before they could speak. There’s something cathartic about sitting in a dark theater with other people, crying together and sharing the same emotions. You feel safe because everyone is experiencing that grief together. I think young people have fewer opportunities to experience cinema that way now. That’s what made these screenings so special.

Die Kunst der Woche in Berlin, Karlsruhe, Hamburg, London, München und Paris

Susan Hiller in Berlin

Was passiert, wenn man lange genug auf einen flackernden Fernsehbildschirm starrt? Vielleicht sieht man irgendwann Geister. In den 1980er-Jahren kursierten tatsächlich Berichte über gespenstische Erscheinungen auf TV-Geräten nach Sendeschluss. Für die Künstlerin Susan Hiller war das ein gefundenes Fressen: Sie machte den Fernseher zum modernen Kaminfeuer, vor dem sich allerlei Fantasien entfalten. Überhaupt hatte die 2019 verstorbene Britin eine Schwäche für alles, was sich einer vernünftigen Erklärung entzieht: UFOs, Nahtoderfahrungen, Spukgeschichten und Menschen, die angeblich schweben können. "Ich habe mich der Arbeit mit 'Geistern' verschrieben", sagte sie einmal.

In ihrer ersten Berliner Überblicksausstellung "Bad Dreams" bei KW begegnet man nun einer Wand aus alten Röhrenfernsehern, aus denen Menschen von Begegnungen mit dem Jenseits erzählen, Fotografien scheinbar schwereloser Körper und Kindern mit übernatürlichen Fähigkeiten. Ob das alles wirklich passiert ist, interessierte Hiller weniger als die Frage, warum wir solche Geschichten erzählen und so gern an das Unheimliche glauben. Außerdem eröffnen die Ausstellungen "Ousssean" der südkoreanischen Künstlerin Koo Jeong A sowie Rafik Greiss' "The City and the City".

Susan Hiller "Bad Dreams" , Koo Jeong A "Ousssean" , Rafik Greiss "The City and the City" , KW Institute of Contemporary Art, Berlin, 17. Oktober bis 10. Januar 2027

Contemporary African Art Fair in London

Parallel zur Frieze kommt an diesem Wochenende die 1-54 Contemporary Art Fair für Kunst aus Afrika und der afrikanischen Diaspora zum 14. Mal nach London – mit einer Neuerung: Als Reaktion auf das wachsende Interesse am afrikanischen Modernismus widmet die Messe im Somerset House der Kunst der Moderne einen eigenen Schwerpunkt. Kuratierte Messekojen präsentieren Meister des 20. Jahrhunderts wie Seyni Awa Camara aus dem Senegal, Aubrey Williams aus Guyana, Tahia Halim aus Ägypten und Twins Seven Seven aus Nigeria.

Ergänzt wird der Schwerpunkt durch die von der Kunsthistorikerin Nancy Dantas kuratierte Gruppenausstellung "West Wind". Ein weiterer Fokus liegt auf Künstlerinnen: Die Londoner Gillian Jason Gallery und O’DA Art aus Lagos widmen ihre Präsentationen ausschließlich weiblichen Kunstschaffenden.

"1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair" , London, bis 18. Oktober

Open Art in München

Die Open Art Munich zählt zu den traditionsreichsten Veranstaltungen ihrer Art: Seit 1989 laden die Münchner Galerien zum Saisonstart im Herbst zu einem gemeinsamen Ausstellungswochenende ein. In diesem Jahr findet es im Oktober parallel zur Messe Munich Highlights statt. An diesem Wochenende öffnen rund 50 Galerien ihre Türen und laden zum Rundgang ein. Bei Walter Storms präsentiert der konzeptionelle Bildhauer und Objektkünstler Gerold Miller neue Werkgruppen in drei Galerieräumen. In der Galerie Klüser erkunden Lori Nix und Isca Greenfield-Sanders mit fotografischen und malerischen Arbeiten die instabile Konstruktion von Wirklichkeit. Ein Highlight im Bereich der jungen Kunst ist die Ausstellung von Sophia Mainka in der Galerie The Tiger Room.

Open Art Munich , München, bis 18. Oktober

Neues Museum Large in Paris

Begrünte Terrassen, Uferpromenaden und ein elegantes Gebäude, in dessen Kupferfassade das Sonnenlicht spielt: Man muss die Augen schon sehr eng zusammenkneifen, um sich auszumalen, dass die Île Seguin bei Paris vor nicht allzu langer Zeit noch ein gigantischer Industriestandort war. Fast 70 Jahre lang betrieb der Autobauer Renault auf der Seine-Insel eine der größten und modernsten Fabriken der Welt. Nach der Schließung und dem Abriss der Gebäude im Jahr 2005 wollte sich Luxusmogul François Pinault hier ein Privatmuseum von Tadao Ando bauen lassen – er scheiterte an der Bürokratie.

Vier Jahre später wurde der Architekt Jean Nouvel mit dem Masterplan für ein Kulturquartier beauftragt. Der erste Meilenstein war ein Musikzentrum, der zweite folgt ab Samstag mit der Eröffnung eines Zentrums für zeitgenössische Kunst namens Large. Der von RCR Arquitectes (Pritzker-Preis 2017) entworfene Bau umfasst 5000 Quadratmeter. Die von Cecilia Alemani kuratierte Auftaktschau "Moteur Imaginaire" beleuchtet die Verbindungen zwischen Mensch und Maschine. In Zusammenarbeit mit dem Renault-Fonds für Kunst und Kultur stellt sie historische Meisterwerke von Vasarely, Dubuffet, Tinguely und Doisneau in einen Dialog mit 17 Auftragsarbeiten zeitgenössischer Künstler wie Théo Mercier, Sara Sadik oder Bertrand Lavier.

"Imaginary Engine" , Large – Zentrum für zeitgenössische Kunst Île Seguin, Paris, 17. Oktober bis 7. März 2027

Fake News in Hamburg

Wie sich Nachrichten in Zeiten von Desinformation, künstlicher Intelligenz und sozialen Medien verändern, zeigt eine neue Ausstellung im Hamburger Museum der Arbeit. Die Schau " Nachrichten – News" beleuchte dabei nicht nur die Geschichte der Nachrichten , sondern auch die Arbeit der Menschen, die hinter den Nachrichten stehen, sagte Kuratorin Sandra Schürmann. Beide Perspektiven würden eingenommen: die der Nachrichtenproduzenten und der Nachrichtenkonsumenten.

Vor dem Hintergrund eines schwindenden Vertrauens in die Medien behandele die Ausstellung "topaktuelle Themen", sagte Museumsdirektorin Rita Müller. "Es geht um den Umgang mit Informationen, mit Nachrichten , es geht um Desinformation, Fake News, Glaubwürdigkeit, Vertrauen, es geht um Pressefreiheit und schließlich geht es auch um unsere Demokratie."

Besuchern wird ein Blick hinter die Kulissen verschiedener Medien und die Arbeit von Agenturen, Korrespondenten und Redaktionen geboten. Die interaktiven und multimedialen Angebote richten sich an alle Altersgruppen ab der neunten Klasse.

"Nachrichten – News" , Museum der Arbeit, Hamburg, bis 16. Mai 2027

Mars-Performance in Karlsruhe

Tütennahrung, Konservenfutter, manchmal auch frittierte Insekten und das Ganze unter ständiger Beobachtung durch Passanten – auf dem Karlsruher Marktplatz startet eine Marsmission der besonderen Art. In eine extra dafür aufgebaute und mit einer weißen Plane bedeckte Metallkuppel ziehen Künstlerinnen, Künstler und Mitarbeiter des Zentrums für Kunst und Medien (ZKM) ein und simulieren darin in einer Art Dauerperformance das Leben auf einer Marsstation.

Immer drei Personen in wechselnder Besetzung sollen dabei im "Red Dust City" genannten Habitat bestimmte Aufgaben erfüllen und etwa erforschen, wie sich Zusammenleben gestalten lässt, wie man mit Ressourcen wie Wasser umgeht oder wie man nachhaltig leben kann. Interessierte oder zufällig vorbeilaufende Passanten können die ZKM-Crew durch ein etwa zwei Meter großes Guckloch-Fenster beobachten oder durch eine transparente Tür hereinschauen, wie ein ZKM-Sprecher erläuterte. Wie die Crew schläft, sich wäscht oder auf die Toilette geht, sei neugierigen Blicken aber entzogen.

Die Ergebnisse der mehrtägigen Aktion seien natürlich nicht für eine mögliche spätere Besiedelung des Mars gedacht. Sondern sie dienten dazu, den Blick auf den Umgang der Menschen mit der Erde zu lenken, die zunehmend unbewohnbar werde, hieß es weiter. Nach einem streng getakteten Zeitplan heißt es für das jeweils in der Kuppel wohnende Trio dann Tag für Tag: Frühstück, Forschung, Bewegung und Mittagessen, Forschung, Abendessen und ins Bett gehen. Für sogenannte Außeneinsätze darf die Crew die Kuppel manchmal auch verlassen – und wird sich dann ohne Kontakt zu den Passanten drumherum in Astronautenanzügen über den Marktplatz bewegen. (dpa)

article_text:
On October 30 of last year, we lost one of cinema’s most daring auteurs: the British director Peter Watkins. Starting out in television in the 1960s, Watkins developed an utterly unique and militantly political mode of filmmaking. In works like Culloden (1964) , The War Game (1966) , Punishment Park (1971) , and his magnum opus, La Commune (Paris, 1871) (2000), he cast nonprofessional actors in enactments of political events from the past, present, or a dystopian future, which he then shot in the style of live news reporting on TV. The results are thrilling films that startle with their naturalism and urgency, and provoke thorny questions about authoritarianism—not just of the state, but also of the media.

To commemorate this great filmmaker’s legacy, Film Comment editor Devika Girish invited critic J. Hoberman, who has not only admired and written about Watkins’s work, but also took a class with the man himself back in the 1970s. They talk about the trajectory of Watkins’s life and work, what makes his films feel so singular even today, and the contemporary directors that carry forward his legacy.

Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Cannes coverage. The film arrives in theaters on November 6.

It’s never wise to assume anything. Promotional materials doing the rounds before Club Kid ‘s raucous Cannes premiere this week suggested a New York downtown scene answer to Mia Hansen-Løve’s Eden , but Jordan Firstman’s funny, bittersweet, and tremendously moving directorial debut is as much a fresh reimagining of the stunted father subgenre that gave us everything from Kramer vs Kramer and Marriage Story to Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy . This is a movie that promises and delivers scenes of copious drug taking and gross-out comedy, but its third-act emotional payoff is as earned and devastating as the best of them.

For fans who’ve followed Firstman’s career from Rotting in the Sun to I Love LA , this duck-to-water move behind the camera will come as a welcome surprise. It’s notable that the movie opened in Un Certain Regard, a sidebar the festival’s programmers have often used as a testing ground for movie stars looking to try their hand at the tiller for the first time. The difference with Firstman’s confident arrival is that it feels less the work of a dilettante than a natural. Just look at Club Kid ‘s opening sequence, which opens on a fluid and immersive “oner” by cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra (who shot The Studio and The Last Black Man in San Francisco ) that takes us from the front seat of an Uber all the way onto the dancefloor of Club Labor, where Peter Green (Firstman) and his entourage are greeted like Henry Hill at the Copacobana. It’s 2016 and the party’s just getting started. But soon the movie wakes up in the present day, a few thousand mornings after the morning after—an alerting choice and the first glimmer of Club Kid ‘s larger ambitions.

The next comes a few scenes later with the abrupt arrival of an English lad named Arlo (Reggie Absolom), a ten-year-old from London who was conceived during a drug-fuelled moment between Peter and an English tourist on that fateful 2016 night. It’s here that Club Kid begins its unlikely journey into the lineage of those Hoffman and Sandler classics, becoming a story less about an aging party boy than a underqualified man coming face to face with the realities of fatherhood for the first time. Been-there, done-that? Perhaps. But no other movie in this subgenre has yet, to my knowledge, contained a scene in which father and son sing Ethel Cain in duet on piano, or the wisdom that fisting can be “lowkey spiritual,” or that a cocktail of G and alcohol is rarely (if ever) advisable.

Those moments and sharp-witted snatches of dialogue are just some of many things that make Club Kid such an engrossing and enjoyable watch—a movie with a clear sense of place and lived experience and packed to the brim with great music (Arthur Russell and Elliott Smith both feature) and personality. For the latter, there is Peter’s lively milieu, which boasts enough girls, gays, and theys to fill a movie twice this size. The movie of course revels in that world of joyful debauchery in its first half, which makes it doubly gratifying that, even after Arlo’s arrival and Peter’s inevitable decision to clean up his act, that the movie never once wags a finger at the life and people being left behind. When a bleary-eyed Peter tells his coked-up business partner Sophie (Cara Delevingne) that he’s turned to dealing drugs at the club partially to keep the community safe, there’s more than an ounce of truth to it—even if we know that, by the laws of screenwriting, those choices will inevitably come back to bite him. As with any well-worn genre piece, you’ll see story beats coming a mile away, but I welcomed their arrival with open arms.

Add to this a refreshing amount of real bustling streets and choice locations (a lunch scene at Balthazar here, a walk by the East River there, an always welcome shot of the city’s skyline from the window of a car at night) and you end up with one of the best (at least from this outsider’s perspective) New York movies of this scale since at least Past Lives . In a deceptively challenging lead role, Firstman locates an emotional register that feels perfectly in-step with his natural gifts as a comedic actor, and he’s backed by a supporting cast that includes Babylon ’s hunky Diego Calva as a love interest, Hollywood veteran Colleen Camp as an eccentric neighbor, and—naturally—a who’s-who of the downtown scene (keep an eye out for Nick Pinkerton). Delevingne can chew scenery a bit much for comfort and I probably could have done without Arlo’s DJ subplot (which, as Peter notes, is indeed “lowkey corny”) but Club Kid looks every inch the work of a mature, gifted filmmaker with plenty to say and the guts to lay it all out.

Club Kid premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.

General information

Website

Entrance fee US$50

For additional questions, email to info@smithfund.org

Timeline

Call for entries open – 02 July 2024

Waiver Deadline – 24 September 2024

Submission deadline – 08 October 2024 at 11:59 pm EDT

Grant recipients announced – 10 December 2024

45th Annual W. Eugene Smith Grant Ceremony – TBD

The W. Eugene Smith Grant is designed to encourage and support visual storytellers whose photographic work renews the tradition of W. Eugene Smith’s dedicated compassion as evidenced during his 45-year career as a photographic essayist. Special consideration will be given to work that promotes social change, that embraces new technologies and image distribution, and that seeks to integrate the tradition of photography and social change with contemporary practice. The judges will be looking for a photographer and project that seem most likely to use exemplary and compelling photojournalism and documentary photography (possibly supplemented by or incorporating multi-media) to address an issue of import and impact related to the human condition: social change, humanitarian concern, armed conflict, or other topics of interpersonal, psychological, cultural, social, environmental, scientific, medical and/or political significance, ideally expressing an underlying acknowledgement of our common humanity.

For 2024, the amount of the W. Eugene Smith Grant is $30,000. In addition, two $10,000 Finalist Grant will be awarded

A fee waiver of US$50 will be granted to a selected number of photographers in Southeast Asia upon request sent to Matca via email at hello@matca.vn.

editorial_title_zh: 尤金·布丹展：印象派之父——追寻光芒
editorial_excerpt_zh: 本展旨在介绍被称为“印象派先驱”与“印象派之父”的19世纪法国画家尤金·布丹（1824-1898）的艺术生涯。布丹以清新明快的色彩和轻快流畅的笔触表现故乡诺曼底的天空、海景以及牧场上的牛群而闻名。通过在户外直接观察自然，描绘瞬息万变的光线与大气，这种创作手法对包括年轻克劳德·莫奈在内的当时许多画家产生了巨大影响，并最终促成了印象派的诞生。View More > The post ウジェーヌ・ブーダン展 印象派の父 ― 光を求めて first appeared on ART iT（アートイット） .

article_text:
国際芸術祭「あいち2028」の会期・会場が決定。半田市と名古屋・内田橋地区が初の舞台に

国際芸術祭「 あいち 2028」の会期と会場が発表された。2028年9月16日から12月3日まで、愛知芸術文化センターに加え、初の主会場となる半田市と名古屋市南区の内田橋地区を舞台に開催される。

3年ごとに開催される国際芸術祭「 あいち 」の次回展「あいち2028」の会期と会場が、11月10日に発表された。会期は2028年9月16日（土）から12月3日（日）までの79日間。愛知芸術文化センター、半田市、名古屋市南区の内田橋地区を主な会場として開催される。

愛知芸術文化センターは、2010年の初開催以来、毎回会場となってきた。1992年に名古屋市中心部に開館した複合文化施設で、国内外の20世紀美術を中心とする充実したコレクションを擁する愛知県美術館、大ホールやコンサートホール、小ホールなどを備えた愛知県芸術劇場、アートスペースとアートプラザで構成される愛知県文化情報センターからなる。

今回初めて主会場となる半田市は、名古屋市中心部から南へ約25キロに位置する、知多半島の中心都市だ。天然の良港である衣浦港を生かし、江戸時代から海運や醸造業で栄え、地域の政治・経済・文化の中核として発展してきた。黒板塀の醸造蔵が並ぶ半田運河や、明治期の産業遺産である半田赤レンガ建物などで知られ、童話「ごんぎつね」の作者・新美南吉が生まれ育った地でもある。

同じく初めて主会場となる内田橋地区は、名古屋市南区の北西部に位置する。かつて周辺には遠浅の海が広がり、江戸時代から交通・水運の要所として栄えた。堀川と新堀川が合流する付近に架かる内田橋のたもとには、昔ながらの風情を残す内田橋商店街が広がる。近年は地域住民や商店主による活性化の取り組みが進み、老舗と新たな店舗が共存するまちとなっている。

会場の決定にあたり、芸術監督のシャビール・フセイン・ムスタファは、プレスリリースで次のようにコメントしている。

「これらの場所を訪れ、それぞれの場所がその歴史をいかにして現在へと繋いできたかに感銘を受けました。愛知芸術文化センターは、文化芸術の交流の場として長らく機能しています。内田橋地区では、地域に親しまれてきた建物やスペースに新たな活用の方法を見出す人々と出会いました。半田市では、長く続く醸造と発酵の文化が、まちなかの建物や運河にその歴史を刻んでいます。

アーティストや『あいち2028』のチームをはじめとした仲間たち、そして地域のコミュニティと協働すること、また、これらの出会いを通じてなにが形作られていくかを楽しみにしています」

article_text:
A retrospective for Eva Gonzalès , who is today best known as Édouard Manet’s only formal pupil, has been long overdue. That correction was planned for 2020, when the Château-Musée de Dieppe was to organize a show as part of the Normandie Impressionniste festival, but it was put on hold by the pandemic until the Petit Palais took up the mantle, where “Eva Gonzalès (1847–1883): A Free-Spirited Artist’s Journey” is on view until January.

The six-year delay turned out to be fortuitous, according to cocurator Stéphanie Cantarutti. Now, Manet’s Portrait of Eva Gonzalès (1870) from the National Gallery and Gonzalès’s Une loge aux Italiens (ca. 1874) from the Musée d’Orsay, can be included, as can Gonzalès’s Le Moineau (ca. 1865-70), which the curatorial team managed to track down after decades of its whereabouts being unknown. One of some 70 works by her now on view, that delicate portrait of a young girl with a sparrow shows her mastery in pastel. “In the end, time worked in our favor,” Cantarutti told ARTnews .

The exhibition brings further discoveries, including a revision of the artist’s birth year. “What tipped us off was the way the date was written on the birth certificate,” Cantarutti said. “After taking a closer look at the document, we realized that she had been born in 1847, not 1849.” In-depth research also led to the redating and renaming of several paintings: La Fenêtre (1869–70), for example, was renamed Le Catéchisme , while La Psyché , now dated to 1868–69, had previously been dated to 1869–70.

For more than a century, since critic Camille Laurent Mauclair associated Gonzalès with Impressionism in 1904, the artist’s work has regularly been assessed and reassessed through this lens. A 1993 exhibition at Paris’s Musée Marmottan Monet, which presented her alongside Impressionism’s two most famous women artists, Mary Cassatt and Berthe Morisot, was instrumental in reinforcing this association. The Petit Palais exhibition, however, takes a different approach.

“I am personally opposed to this affiliation,” Cantarutti said. “I fought to ensure that the term ‘Impressionism’ would not appear in any communication materials. The exhibition in no way presents her as an Impressionist.”

There is art historical truth to that statement, as Gonzalès never participated in any of the Impressionist exhibitions. “Her strategy was, like Manet’s, to establish herself at the Salon,” conservator Marianne Mathieu said, noting that Berthe Morisot, against Manet’s advice, turned her back on the Salon and joined the cooperative society whose members would soon become known as the Impressionists.

Gonzalès and Morisot had much in common: They came from cultivated bourgeois families, were criticized for their fierce independence, used their sisters as models, continued to sign their maiden names after marriage, and were close friends with Manet. Morisot, however, further resisted Manet’s tutelage all the more after he substantially retouched one of her paintings in 1870, whereas Gonzalès would ultimately embrace his guidance. “Morisot sought to emancipate herself from the very idea of artistic affiliation, even if that meant becoming part of an emerging avant-garde,” added Mathieu. “Gonzalès, by contrast, boldly claimed her allegiance to Manet, who was a controversial figure at the time.”

The Gonzalès retrospective also raises the question of why this allegiance remained largely concealed for part of her early career. Gonzalès left the studio of Charles Chaplin, her first teacher who did not think a single woman should have her own studio, in 1868 and became Manet’s pupil the following year, after the two met at the salon of painter Alfred Stevens. Gonzalès’s pedagogical roots were further muddied when she submitted to the 1870 Salon. She registered as Chaplin’s pupil, but Enfant de troupe (1869–70) , one of two paintings selected, clearly drew on Manet’s Le Fifre (1866) . Depicting a young boy in military uniform holding a bugle against a dark, neutral background, Enfant de troupe was acquired by the French State, the only work of hers to enter a public collection during her lifetime, and the acquisition likely owed much to the connections of her father, prominent writer Emmanuel Gonzalès.

Further complicating the situation, Manet exhibited at the 1870 Salon his 6.25-foot-tall Portrait d’Eva Gonzalès . The novelist and journalist Armand Lapointe, a family friend, called the portrait a failure and reproached Gonzalès for having agreed to sit for Manet. Ironically, in 1874, the first year she came registered as Manet’s pupil at the Salon, her submission, Une loge aux Italiens , of a man and woman seated in a theater box, was rejected by the jury.

It is difficult to assess Gonzalès’s style, as she died too young—at 36, with the revised birth year—to reveal the full extent of her abilities. She confined herself to the subjects traditionally deemed appropriate for women artists at the time: portraits of family and friends, scenes of domestic life and leisure, and still lifes. Such subjects helped her avoid controversy and establish a reputation. According to critic Jean-Marie Tasset, “Behind her intimate scenes and landscapes lies a fierce energy, a blazing fire that reveals itself as soon as Eva sets her brush to canvas. All the dark magic of the blue note.” Under Manet’s aegis, her style grew more spontaneous. How brightly and freely her flame might have burned had she lived longer remains an open question.

At the Petit Palais, visitors follow a broadly chronological path through Gonzalès’s career, with thematic digressions exploring her relationship with her husband, Henri Guérard, and their artistic partnership, including time spent together in Normandy. A renowned beauty with a slender figure and an elegant wardrobe evocative of her social status, Gonzalès had rejected eligible suitors before falling in love with Guérard, a talented engraver who collaborated with Manet, Paul Gachet, Camille Pissarro, and Paul Cezanne, among others. The couple married in 1879 and remained together until Gonzalès’s death in 1883. Guérard later remarried his sister-in-law Jeanne, which Gonzalès seems to have predicted in her rejected-Salon painting, Une loge aux Italiens : the man and woman are, in fact, Guérard and Jeanne. “There is material for a great movie scenario, for sure,” Cantarutti said. “We, however, chose to stick to the facts.”

The final section unfolds in two parts. One looks beyond Gonzalès’s death, bringing together pastels of Jeanne posing in Eva’s wedding dress (perhaps another premonition on Gonzalès’s part), photographs of Gonzalès’s 1885 posthumous retrospective, and a Norbert Goeneutte portrait of Eva’s son, Jean-Raimond.

The other half focuses on the artist’s final works, including Miss et Bébé (1877–78) featuring a nanny watching over a little girl. “We can see the evolution from the porcelain-like finish of compositions in the style of Chaplin toward a more energetic touch,” Cantarutti said. “In unfixed pastel-on-canvas works held in the United States, her use of increasingly bold colors is striking, along with a greater freedom in her brushwork.” In Pommes d’Api , which is owned by the Minneapolis Institute of Art and was too fragile to bring to Paris, the brightness of Gonzalès’s reds and yellows convey the apples’ acidity.

What accounts Gonzalès’s near absence from most art historical tellings of late 19th-century French art? The exhibition shows that she enjoyed considerable success during her lifetime, and Jean-Raimond Guérard tried to keep the contributions of his mother in the conversation as much as he could. But unlike Julie Manet, Berthe Morisot’s daughter, he alone was working to keep alive Gonzalès’s legacy, according to Cantarutti. Julie Manet was surrounded by figures like Stéphane Mallarmé, Claude Monet, and Edgar Degas, who helped her elevate Morisot’s status as a preeminent Impressionist, as did her husband, Ernest Rouart, who was at the same time fighting to secure recognition for his father’s collection and work.

Cantarutti offered a second reason: “She is not that heavily represented in French national museums.” The Musée d’Orsay has La Matinée rose ( The Pink Morning ), a 1874 pastel acquired by the French state in 1885. More than 135 years would pass before the Petit Palais purchased the oil painting La Servante or À la barrière (ca. 1865-70) in 2021. (“Most of her works are now in private collections, scattered across France and abroad,” Cantarutti noted.)

Gonzalès has often been described in relation to others—as someone’s daughter or someone’s pupil—and much has been made of the connections that linked her to this artistic and literary milieu. “What struck me, however, was that she was interesting in her own right,” said Cantarutti, who sees the exhibition as a first step toward more recognition and research. “With more than a hundred works, including roughly two-thirds by her, we have never been so close to recreating the scale of the 1885 retrospective. It is a chance for the public to discover what a remarkable artist she was—and I think people will be pleasantly surprised.”

連続テレビ小説「ブラッサム」

＜総合＞【毎週月曜～土曜】 午前8時～8時15分＊土曜は1週間を振り返ります ＜NHK BS＞【毎週月曜～金曜】午前7時30分～7時45分 ＜BSP4K＞【毎週月曜～金曜】午前7時30分～7時45分

【作】 櫻井 剛、小松與志子 【音楽】 fox capture plan 【主題歌】 「咲き誇れ」 YOASOBI 【出演】 石橋静河、加賀まりこ、松たか子、国仲涼子、渡部篤郎 ほか 【スタッフ】 制作統括：村山峻平、櫻井壮一 プロデューサー：大野陽平 演出：盆子原 誠、中泉 慧、佐藤玲衣、田中陽児、小林直毅、野田雄介

公式サイト 公式X 公式Instagram

第６週 「ふたり、北へ」

お腹に赤ん坊が宿っていることが分かり、喜ぶ珠（石橋静河）と保（金子大地）。しかし、保が大学に通いながら生活費をどう工面するかなど、考えなければいけない問題は山積みであった。そんな中、札幌の銀行に勤める保の親戚、木村正吾（三宅弘城）が照子（山田真歩）と一緒に突然、訪ねてくる。照子と正吾は、珠と保に必要な出産費用や生活費の援助をすることを条件に、あることを珠たちに提案する。
